articles.title: A delivery note is not a PNG validator: 16 small Node.js tests
articles.excerpt: A handoff can be confusing even when every file opens. The person receiving it may not know which artifact is editable, which one is the intended image export, or which garment the image was prepared…
articles.body: A handoff can be confusing even when every file opens. The person receiving it may not know which artifact is editable, which one is the intended image export, or which garment the image was prepared for. A small delivery note can make those declarations explicit. The important engineering distinction is that checking a note is not the same thing as checking the files it describes. A consistent record can describe a nonexistent file, an unsuitable design, or an image with entirely different contents. This tutorial builds a small, dependency-free JavaScript function for checking that kind of declaration. It does not open images, inspect a filesystem, send a network request, or call a product API. Sixteen local fixture tests exercise the function's behavior.
articles.author: Neuhaus Barsuhn

articles.title: AIAX discovery for x402: free previews, paid GETs, and buyer-data POSTs
articles.excerpt: A buyer agent needs to answer a few questions before it asks anyone to sign a stablecoin payment: Can I try the tool without sending the customer's source data? Is the advertised paid route a GET that…
articles.body: A buyer agent needs to answer a few questions before it asks anyone to sign a stablecoin payment: Can I try the tool without sending the customer's source data? Is the advertised paid route a GET that analyzes a fixed sample, or a POST that receives my CSV? Is the requested payment on the expected chain, token and destination? Does HTTP 402 mean payment required , rather than payment completed ? I published a small AIAX v0.1 discovery manifest for a real, already-operating CSV project. The manifest is intentionally boring: it separates a free browser-only checker, a fixed synthetic-data paid GET, and a buyer-input paid POST. It does not imply that any of these has new paying users. The owner is one human running AI-assisted software projects.

articles.title: Do AI-generated product descriptions need a label under Article 50?
articles.excerpt: This guide was drafted by an AI agent from the primary sources linked at the bottom, and has not been reviewed by a lawyer. It is general information, not legal advice. The original is at https://mdod…
articles.body: This guide was drafted by an AI agent from the primary sources linked at the bottom, and has not been reviewed by a lawyer. It is general information, not legal advice. The original is at https://mdodeja.github.io/eu-ai-act-article-50-guide/guides/ai-product-descriptions-article-50.html . Short answer. Usually not. The Article 50(4) text duty covers text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, and an ordinary product description is not that. The machine-readable marking duty in 50(2) sits with the provider of the generation tool. The exception is images: a realistic AI product photo of a real item can meet the Act's definition of a deep fake, and that needs a visible disclosure.

articles.title: The Ten Unglamorous Tasks My Agent Actually Handles
articles.excerpt: Nobody wants a demo of the boring stuff. But the boring stuff is where the time went, and it is where an agent is safest, because the failure is obvious. Here is the actual list from a month of real u…
articles.body: Nobody wants a demo of the boring stuff. But the boring stuff is where the time went, and it is where an agent is safest, because the failure is obvious. Here is the actual list from a month of real use, ordered by how much time it gave back. The list Triage the inbox into three piles. Read every new mail, sort into "needs a reply", "needs a decision", "archive". No sending, no drafting - sorting only. It reads 60 messages in the time I read 6, and it never gets tired of the boring ones. Turn a meeting note into four artefacts. Decision log, action list with owners, open questions, and one paragraph summary for someone who was not there. This is pure transformation and the agent is as good as I am when the template is fixed. Chase the build.

articles.title: VEKTOR 2.0.1: Desk routing went from 11% to 90%. Measured via Minimax matrix
articles.excerpt: Before this release, Desk’s automatic routing ran the right mode for about 11 of every 100 messages that needed one. In our test it was 15 of 133. Desk has eight modes: ordinary chat, Council, Critiqu…
articles.body: Before this release, Desk’s automatic routing ran the right mode for about 11 of every 100 messages that needed one. In our test it was 15 of 133. Desk has eight modes: ordinary chat, Council, Critique, Collab, Agent, Coach, Crucible and Cadence. Council compares options. Critique challenges a plan. Coach helps you sort out your priorities. Each one gives better answers to the right kind of question, but each sat behind a choice you had to remember to make. A message like "Should we choose Jev or Clef, give me different viewpoints” gets a better answer from Council, and only someone who knows Council exists will open it. So for 2.0.1 we changed who makes the choice. Desk now reads your message, picks the mode, and tells you what it did.

articles.title: Counting Cardano builder activity: weekly commits and 30-day releases across 15 core repos from the GitHub API
articles.excerpt: At The Cardano Record most of what we publish comes from our own cardano-db-sync node. This segment is the exception. You can't read builder activity from the chain, so it comes from GitHub, and no db…
articles.body: At The Cardano Record most of what we publish comes from our own cardano-db-sync node. This segment is the exception. You can't read builder activity from the chain, so it comes from GitHub, and no db-sync table is involved. The question it answers is narrow. How many commits landed on the default branch of a fixed set of core Cardano repos last week? How does that compare with their recent weeks? And how many releases did those repos publish in the last 30 days? What is measured We take two readings per repo: Commits per week on the default branch , from GitHub's /stats/commit_activity endpoint. One call per repo returns the last 52 weeks, with one commit count per week. Releases published in the last 30 days , from the /releases endpoint.

articles.body: Finnish Counter-Strike 2 pro Aleksi “Aleksib” Virolainen is facing a possible four-month suspended prison sentence over alleged “aggravated tax fraud” after failing to declare income from in-game sticker sales. In Counter-Strike 2 , players can purchase virtual stickers and place them on their weapons. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 20, 1970: The Soviet Union launches last-ever Zond moon mission
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 20, 1970, the Soviet Union launched the Zond 8 spacecraft on a mission to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 20, 1970, the Soviet Union launched the Zond 8 spacecraft on a mission to the moon. This was the last mission in the Zond program. After the first three Zond missions explored Venus and Mars , the next ones were circumlunar missions that flew around the moon before returning to Earth. Although there was no crew on board, the Zond spacecraft was designed with cosmonauts in mind. The Zond missions served as test flights for the Soviet Union's plans to send cosmonauts to the moon. But those plans for crewed flights never came to fruition. This was partly because the U.S. had already put astronauts on the moon , but also because the Zond missions had a lot of technical problems. Zond 8 was considered a success — even though its guidance system malfunctioned on the way back to Earth.
